title: “SPEAK THOSE THINGS THAT ARE NOT AS THOUGH THEY WERE” — ROMANS 4:17 IS NOT TELLING YOU TO MANIFEST YOUR REALITY
paragraphs: “SPEAK THOSE THINGS THAT ARE NOT AS THOUGH THEY WERE” — ROMANS 4:17 IS NOT TELLING YOU TO MANIFEST YOUR REALITY
You were never commanded to create reality with your words. You were invited to trust the God who can create life where there is nothing but death.
There is a Bible verse being passed around like a spiritual blank check.
You may have heard it after losing a job.
“Speak your new job into existence.”
After receiving bad news.
“Don’t say what you see. Speak what you want.”
When money is disappearing faster than it comes in.
“Declare abundance.”
When the relationship is broken.
“Call it restored.”
When the dream seems impossible.
“Speak those things that are not as though they were.”
And then Romans 4:17 gets attached to it.
It sounds biblical.
It sounds powerful.
It sounds like faith.
There is only one problem.
That is not what Romans 4:17 says.
And once you see what Paul actually wrote, the verse becomes far more beautiful than manifestation could ever make it.
Because Romans 4 is not teaching you how to become the creator of your reality.
It is teaching you how to trust the Creator when your reality looks impossible.
Read Paul's words carefully:

“As it is written, ‘I have made you the father of many nations’—in the presence of the God in whom he believed, who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist.” — Romans 4:17, ESV
Now look at the crucial words in Greek:
θεοῦ τοῦ ζῳοποιοῦντος τοὺς νεκροὺς καὶ καλοῦντος τὰ μὴ ὄντα ὡς ὄντα
theou tou zōopoiountos tous nekrous kai kalountos ta mē onta hōs onta
The heart of the sentence is staggering.
God is the One “giving life to the dead” and “calling the things that are not as though they are.”
Notice who is doing the calling.
God.
Not Abraham.
Not Sarah.
Not you.
Not me.
God.
That one observation changes everything.
Romans 4:17 does not say, “Abraham called things that were not as though they were.”
Paul describes God as the One who does this.

The popular expression “speak those things that are not as though they were” can therefore become seriously misleading when it is presented as a command for Christians to verbally manufacture desired circumstances.
The verse is not giving humanity God's creative authority.
It is revealing the character of the God Abraham trusted.
And maybe that disappoints part of you.
Because manifestation offers something incredibly attractive.
Control.
Say the correct words.
Think the correct thoughts.
Maintain the correct energy.
Refuse negative confessions.
Visualize hard enough.
Declare consistently enough.
And eventually reality supposedly has to cooperate.
But biblical faith is different.
Biblical faith does not put reality under your authority.
Biblical faith puts you under God's authority while teaching you to trust Him in the middle of reality.
That is harder.
And infinitely safer.
Because sometimes you can speak faithfully and still walk through suffering.
Sometimes you can pray desperately and the answer is not the answer you wanted.
Sometimes the diagnosis remains.
Sometimes the person leaves.
Sometimes the business fails.
Sometimes the door stays closed.
Sometimes you bury someone you begged God to heal.
And if Christianity has been reduced to “your words create your world,” what happens then?
You begin blaming yourself.
Maybe I spoke negatively.
Maybe I doubted.
Maybe my faith wasn't strong enough.
Maybe I ruined my miracle.
And now suffering has acquired another wound:
shame.
But look at Abraham.
Paul is not describing a man pretending reality didn't exist.
He is describing a man staring directly at an impossible reality while trusting a God greater than it.
Romans 4:19 says Abraham considered the condition of his own body, which was “as good as dead,” since he was about a hundred years old, and he considered Sarah's barrenness.
Abraham knew what his body was telling him.
He knew Sarah's history.
He knew the mathematics.
He knew the biology.
Faith did not require him to become delusional.
Faith required him to decide whether God's promise was more trustworthy than his circumstances were powerful.
That distinction matters.
Christian faith is not denying facts.
It is refusing to make facts greater than God.
There are facts.
And then there is God.
Cancer can be a fact.
Debt can be a fact.
Infertility can be a fact.
Grief can be a fact.
Betrayal can be a fact.
A shattered marriage can be a fact.
Your own terrible decisions can be facts.
The Gospel never requires you to rename darkness “light” just to prove you have faith.
Scripture repeatedly teaches God's people to tell the truth.
The Psalms are filled with people crying, grieving, questioning, confessing, pleading, and lamenting before God.
Jesus Himself prayed in Gethsemane:
“My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.” — Matthew 26:39, ESV
Think about that prayer.
Jesus did not “manifest” another outcome.
He surrendered Himself to the Father.
“Not as I will, but as You will.”
That sentence demolishes the idea that mature spirituality means forcing reality to conform to personal desire.
The center of Christianity is not the sovereignty of your desires.
It is the lordship of Jesus Christ.
And this is where the message becomes uncomfortable.
Because manifestation spirituality can dress itself in Christian vocabulary while quietly moving the center of faith.
God becomes the mechanism.
Your dream becomes the destination.
Faith becomes the technique.
Words become the instrument.
And you remain at the center.
But Christianity begins with something radically different:
Jesus is Lord.
Not my vision.
Not my preferred future.
Not my timetable.
Not my declaration.
Jesus.
Biblical confession certainly matters.
Words matter.
Prayer matters.
Hope matters.
Faith matters.
Scripture even teaches believers to ask God boldly.
But asking God boldly is not the same thing as commanding reality independently.
Jesus taught His disciples to pray:
“Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven.” — Matthew 6:10, ESV
There it is again.
Your will.
Christian prayer is bold without becoming sovereign.
Confident without becoming controlling.
Expectant without pretending God owes us our preferred outcome.
We can pray for healing.
We can pray for provision.
We can pray for reconciliation.
We can ask God to open doors no human being could open.
We can believe that God still does what appears impossible.
Romans 4 absolutely encourages that kind of faith.
But our confidence rests in God, not in some supposed metaphysical power hidden inside our vocabulary.
Abraham's greatness in Romans 4 was not that he discovered how to manipulate the universe.
It was that he believed God.
Romans 4:20–21 says:
“No unbelief made him waver concerning the promise of God, but he grew strong in his faith as he gave glory to God, fully convinced that God was able to do what he had promised.” — ESV
Read the last part again.
God was able to do what God had promised.
That is the engine of Abraham's faith.
Not:
“I am able to create whatever I repeatedly declare.”
But:
“God is able to do what He has promised.”
That is an enormous difference.
Biblical faith does not begin by asking, “What reality do I want to create?”
It asks, “What has God actually promised?”
Because God has never promised to obey every dream we attach His name to.
Sometimes the thing you desperately want is not what He has promised.
And sometimes His mercy appears in the very door you begged Him to open remaining shut.
You may not understand that immediately.
Joseph probably did not understand the pit.
David probably did not understand years of running from Saul.
Paul asked for his thorn to leave and instead heard:
“My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” — 2 Corinthians 12:9, ESV
Paul did not fail manifestation.
He encountered sufficient grace.
There is a world of difference.
Perhaps you have been exhausting yourself trying to control tomorrow with today's declarations.
Perhaps you are afraid that admitting fear will create something bad.
Perhaps somebody convinced you that acknowledging pain is a “negative confession.”
So you learned to smile while bleeding.
You learned to call yourself victorious while privately collapsing.
You learned Christian vocabulary without Christian surrender.
And somewhere beneath all those declarations is a frightened human being whispering:
“What if I can't make this happen?”
Here is the freedom Romans 4 gives you.
You don't have to.
You were never God.
You were never supposed to carry God's job.
You cannot speak creation into existence the way the Creator can.
You cannot guarantee tomorrow.
You cannot control every outcome.
You cannot manipulate Providence by arranging sentences correctly.
But you can know the One who holds tomorrow.
And that is better.
Abraham's story ultimately leads beyond Abraham.
Paul's argument does not end with Isaac.
It moves toward Jesus.
Romans 4:23–25 explains that the righteousness credited to Abraham was written also for those who believe in the God who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead.
Suddenly Romans 4:17 becomes even more breathtaking.
The God “who gives life to the dead” is the God who raised Jesus Christ.
Christianity is built upon resurrection.
Not manifestation.
Resurrection.
Manifestation says, in effect, “Use your inner power to bring your desired future into reality.”
The Gospel announces something altogether different:
You were spiritually helpless, and God acted to save.
Jesus entered our scandal.
Our rebellion.
Our guilt.
Our shame.
Our death.
He carried sin to the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
And God raised Him from the dead.
We didn't manifest salvation.
We needed rescue.
We didn't declare ourselves righteous until heaven accepted the vocabulary.
Christ became our righteousness.
We didn't speak our sins out of existence.
Jesus shed His blood for sinners.
That is why grace is so offensive to human pride.
Grace means you cannot save yourself.
But grace is also breathtakingly beautiful for exactly the same reason.
You don't have to.
Maybe your life right now doesn't resemble the testimony you imagined you would have.
Maybe your marriage has scars.
Maybe your children have wandered.
Maybe addiction left wreckage behind.
Maybe pornography has become the secret room nobody knows exists.
Maybe you smile at church while wondering whether God could possibly still want you.
Maybe your bank account terrifies you.
Maybe your prayers seem to hit the ceiling.
Maybe you keep declaring victory because you're terrified to admit:
“God, I'm tired.”
Say it.
He already knows.
Biblical faith can survive honesty.
David's did.
Job's did.
Jeremiah's did.
Peter's did.
Because faith is not pretending everything is okay.
Faith is bringing everything that is not okay to the God who remains faithful.
And perhaps the greatest “thing that is not” in your story is not the house you want, the promotion you want, the relationship you want, or the money you want.
Maybe what looks impossible is you.
The person you have become.
The years you wasted.
The sins nobody knows about.
The marriage you damaged.
The promises you broke.
The secret habits.
The bitterness.
The shame.
The version of yourself you cannot seem to escape.
And now Romans 4:17 suddenly sounds different:
He gives life to the dead.
That is your hope.
Not that you can manifest a better version of yourself.
That Jesus Christ raises dead people.
The Gospel is not self-improvement.
It is resurrection.
Peter denied Jesus and was restored.
Paul persecuted Christians and became an apostle of Christ.
The thief beside Jesus had nothing left to offer—no lifetime to repair, no ministry résumé to build, no reputation to recover—and Christ still promised him paradise.
Scandal.
Then grace.
Failure.
Then mercy.
Death.
Then resurrection.
This is what Jesus does.
He does not pretend the scandal never happened.
He writes grace through it.
That does not mean every earthly consequence disappears. Grace is not permission to continue sinning, nor does forgiveness erase every temporal result of our choices.
But in Christ, sin does not get the final word.
Shame does not get the final word.
Your past does not get the final word.
Death itself does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
So stop trying to become the god of your own universe.
You can finally put that burden down.
You don't need to manifest.
You need to trust.
You don't need magical words.
You need Christ.
You don't need to deny your circumstances.
You need to know that circumstances cannot dethrone your Savior.
You don't need to declare yourself powerful.
You can confess your weakness and discover that His grace is sufficient.
And if you have wandered into spirituality where Jesus became little more than a tool for getting the life you wanted, come home.
Repentance is not humiliation designed to crush you.
It is the mercy of God calling you out of the lie and back toward Christ.
Confess your sin.
Trust the crucified and risen Savior.
Follow Him.
Let His Word correct you even when the correction hurts.
Because sometimes the verse you thought promised you control was actually offering you something better:
God Himself.
When it is, remember the subject of the sentence.
God.
It cannot. Christ cannot be bought, and grace is not merchandise.

Support can, however, help this ministry continue creating and distributing Christ-centered teaching, Gospel encouragement, discipleship resources, and biblical content. One practical way to glorify God is to use what He has entrusted to you to help truthful Gospel ministry reach other people.
But never confuse supporting a ministry with supporting your salvation.
Jesus already paid for that.
And He did not pay fifty percent.
He gave Himself.
So the next time someone tells you Romans 4:17 means you can speak whatever future you desire into existence, remember Abraham standing before an impossible situation.
His hope was never the power of Abraham's mouth.
His hope was the faithfulness of Abraham's God.
And maybe that is exactly what your exhausted soul needed to hear.
You do not have to control tomorrow with your words.
You can entrust tomorrow to the One who walked out of a grave.
You were never given the burden of speaking your reality into existence—you were given the breathtaking privilege of trusting the God who raises the dead.
